title: Judges 9:34–49
context: Abimelech’s forces ambush Gaal, who is taunted by Zebul and defeated outside the gate, then driven from the city. The next day Abimelech attacks the people in the fields, captures Shechem, kills its people, tears down the city, and sows it with salt. When the men of the tower of Shechem take refuge in the stronghold of El-berith, Abimelech’s men pile branches against it and burn it, killing about a thousand men and women. Jotham’s warning of fire is being fulfilled.

verses.text: Abimelech rose up, and all the people who were with him, by night, and they laid wait against Shechem in four companies.
verses.arminianNotes: Abimelech and his people rise by night and lie in wait against Shechem in four companies. Arminian readers note that Abimelech follows Zebul’s advice exactly, showing that his network inside the city still holds.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the coming attack as Abimelech turning on the people who made him king, as Jotham warned. Both traditions read the four companies as a sign of careful preparation for a battle against his own former supporters.

verses.text: Gaal the son of Ebed went out, and stood in the entrance of the gate of the city. Abimelech rose up, and the people who were with him, from the ambush.
verses.arminianNotes: Gaal stands at the city gate as Abimelech’s forces rise from ambush. Arminian readers note the dramatic timing, with Gaal in the place of public authority at the very moment the danger he invited arrives.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the boaster now exposed at the gate, the place where his words will be tested. Shared ground: the narrative builds tension as the two rivals come face to face, with Zebul standing nearby to complete the trap.

verses.text: When Gaal saw the people, he said to Zebul, “Behold, people are coming down from the tops of the mountains.” Zebul said to him, “You see the shadows of the mountains as if they were men.”
verses.arminianNotes: Gaal sees people coming down the mountains, and Zebul says he sees only shadows. Arminian readers note Zebul’s deception, buying time for Abimelech’s forces to draw closer while Gaal hesitates at the gate.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe the irony that Gaal, who boasted of removing Abimelech, now doubts what he sees. Both traditions read the exchange as Zebul skillfully playing his part in the ambush, using words to delay a response.

verses.text: Gaal spoke again and said, “Behold, people are coming down by the middle of the land, and one company comes by the way of the oak of Meonenim.”
verses.arminianNotes: Gaal insists that people are coming by the middle of the land and by the oak of Meonenim. Arminian readers note that the oak’s name may relate to divination, a hint at the religious practices around Shechem, though the meaning is uncertain.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Gaal growing certain as the danger becomes undeniable. Shared ground: the specific landmarks give the scene vividness, though their exact locations near Shechem cannot be identified with confidence.

verses.text: Then Zebul said to him, “Now where is your mouth, that you said, ‘Who is Abimelech, that we should serve him?’ Isn’t this the people that you have despised? Please go out now and fight with them.”
verses.arminianNotes: Zebul throws Gaal’s boast back at him: where is your mouth now? Arminian readers see a sharp rebuke that forces Gaal to act on his words, leaving him no honorable way to refuse the battle he had demanded.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see pride humbled, as the boaster must now face the army he despised. Both traditions read Zebul’s taunt as the turning point that sends Gaal out to defeat, exposing the emptiness of his earlier challenge.

verses.text: Gaal went out before the men of Shechem, and fought with Abimelech.
verses.arminianNotes: Gaal goes out before the men of Shechem and fights Abimelech. Arminian readers note that he leads Shechem into battle, so the city that chose Abimelech now openly fights him, fulfilling Jotham’s word of mutual destruction.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the fire coming out from the men of Shechem against Abimelech, as Jotham warned (9:20). Shared ground: the battle shows the partnership of 9:6 falling apart into open warfare between former allies.

verses.text: Abimelech chased him, and he fled before him, and many fell wounded, even to the entrance of the gate.
verses.arminianNotes: Abimelech chases Gaal, and many fall wounded up to the gate. Arminian readers note the rout, which ends Gaal’s brief challenge and shows how quickly a movement built on boasting collapses under pressure.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Abimelech’s success as temporary, part of a larger judgment that will reach him too. Both traditions read the defeat at the gate as the end of Gaal’s revolt but not the end of the violence between Abimelech and Shechem.

verses.text: Abimelech lived at Arumah; and Zebul drove out Gaal and his brothers, that they should not dwell in Shechem.
verses.arminianNotes: Abimelech stays at Arumah, and Zebul drives out Gaal and his brothers. Arminian readers note that Arumah’s location is uncertain, though it seems to lie near Shechem, and that Zebul completes the expulsion.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that Abimelech does not reside in Shechem itself, suggesting a strained relationship with the city. Shared ground: Gaal disappears from the story, but the conflict between Abimelech and Shechem continues.

verses.text: On the next day, the people went out into the field; and they told Abimelech.
verses.arminianNotes: The next day the people go out into the fields, and Abimelech is told. Arminian readers note that ordinary life resumes in Shechem, with people returning to their work, unaware of the attack that is coming.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the calm before Abimelech’s full vengeance on the city. Both traditions read the verse as a transition from the defeat of Gaal to Abimelech’s punishment of Shechem as a whole, which follows at once.

verses.text: He took the people and divided them into three companies, and laid wait in the field; and he looked, and behold, the people came out of the city. So, he rose up against them and struck them.
verses.arminianNotes: Abimelech divides his people into three companies, lies in wait, and strikes those coming out of the city. Arminian readers note that he now targets the people of Shechem themselves, not merely Gaal’s followers.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the fire from Abimelech beginning to consume Shechem, as Jotham warned. Shared ground: the attack on people working in the fields shows Abimelech’s ruthlessness toward the very city that had made him king.

verses.text: Abimelech and the companies that were with him rushed forward and stood in the entrance of the gate of the city; and the two companies rushed on all who were in the field and struck them.
verses.arminianNotes: Abimelech holds the city gate while two companies strike those in the field. Arminian readers note the tactical precision, as Abimelech cuts off retreat to the city while his men attack people in the open.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the narrative records the slaughter without praise, letting the violence speak for itself. Both traditions read the scene as Abimelech’s brutal reprisal, carried out with military skill and no restraint.

verses.text: Abimelech fought against the city all that day; and he took the city and killed the people in it. He beat down the city and sowed it with salt.
verses.arminianNotes: Abimelech takes the city, kills its people, beats it down, and sows it with salt. Arminian readers state the destruction plainly and note that sowing with salt was likely a symbolic act declaring the site ruined.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the city that crowned a murderer itself destroyed, fulfilling the curse. Shared ground: the text describes Abimelech’s violence as part of the judgment on Shechem without approving his cruelty, which God also repays.

verses.text: When all the men of the tower of Shechem heard of it, they entered into the stronghold of the house of Elberith.
verses.arminianNotes: The men of the tower of Shechem enter the stronghold of the house of El-berith. Arminian readers note that the name may mean something like “God of the covenant,” probably related to Baal Berith in 9:4.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the irony that people seek refuge in the temple of the god that funded Abimelech’s rise. Both traditions read the stronghold as a place of false security, though the exact relation of the tower to the city is uncertain.

verses.text: Abimelech was told that all the men of the tower of Shechem were gathered together.
verses.arminianNotes: Abimelech is told that the men of the tower are gathered together. Arminian readers note that the information comes to him quickly, showing again how closely he is following events around Shechem.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the gathering as setting up the fulfillment of Jotham’s curse by fire. Shared ground: the verse is a brief transition that brings Abimelech to the tower, where the fable’s image of fire will be literally fulfilled.

verses.text: Abimelech went up to Mount Zalmon, he and all the people who were with him; and Abimelech took an ax in his hand, and cut down a bough from the trees, and took it up, and laid it on his shoulder. Then he said to the people who were with him, “What you have seen me do, make haste, and do as I have done!”
verses.arminianNotes: Abimelech cuts a bough on Mount Zalmon and tells his men to do as he has done. Arminian readers note his leadership by example, here turned to destructive ends, with his men freely following his lead.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see an eerie echo of the fable, as branches from the trees become the fuel for fire. Both traditions read the scene as building toward the burning of the tower, though the location of Mount Zalmon is uncertain.

verses.text: All the people likewise each cut down his bough, followed Abimelech, and put them at the base of the stronghold, and set the stronghold on fire over them, so that all the people of the tower of Shechem died also, about a thousand men and women.
verses.arminianNotes: The people pile branches at the stronghold and set it on fire, and about a thousand men and women die. Arminian readers state the atrocity plainly and note that the text records the deaths of women as well as men.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the fire from Abimelech devouring the men of Shechem, exactly as Jotham’s curse foretold (9:20). Shared ground: the narrative presents this as the fulfillment of the curse, without commending the cruelty of the act.
